This creates a race window (bounded by the restart backoff, up to `backoff_max_ms`) in which a legitimate operator stop/drain of a crashed or compromised server is silently reverted by the health monitor, reconnecting a process the operator explicitly wanted down.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-lifecycle). Failure scenario: Health monitor tick snapshots `dead_servers` (server X has a dead client / Error status) under a read lock, releases the lock, evaluates `should_restart`, then sleeps for the computed backoff (100ms-5000ms by default, configurable higher via policy). While that task is sleeping, the operator (or the dashboard) calls `stop_server("X")` or `drain_server("X", ...)` because the server is misbehaving — this succeeds immediately and sets status=Disconnected. When the backoff sleep elapses, the health-monitor task resumes and unconditionally calls `manager.restart_server(&server_id).await` (line 111) using the stale snapshot — there is no re-check of the server's current status/generation between the sleep and the restart call. `restart_server` itself (mcp.rs `pub async fn restart_server`) also does not check whether the handle is already Disconnected/Draining before proceeding — it unconditionally sets status=Restarting and calls `start_server`, which reconnects using the preserved config. The operator's explicit stop is silently undone and the process respawns. Fix direction: Re-fetch the server's current status (or a monotonically-incrementing per-handle generation/epoch) immediately before the `restart_server` call at mcp_health.rs:111, and skip the restart if it no longer matches the dead/Error state captured in the snapshot (e.g. it is now `Disconnected` or `Draining`). Alternatively, have `restart_server` itself refuse to proceed if the handle's status was changed to `Disconnected`/`Draining` by something other than the health monitor's own transition to `Restarting` — e.g. record an explicit 'user requested stop' flag on the handle that `should_restart`/`restart_server` consults and clears only on an explicit start/restart request.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: Tool routing table (`state.tool_index`) is a single flat namespace — a newly connected server silently hijacks an existing tool name — `connect_server` maintains `state.tool_index: HashMap<String,String>` keyed only by bare tool name, with no per-server namespacing. On collision it logs a warning and lets the newest registration win (`state.tool_index.insert` after only a `warn!`), and this same map is the sole routing table used later by `call_server_tool` to pick which server handles a call. Any MCP server — including one installed after the fact and with a lower trust level — can therefore capture all future dispatch for an existing, common tool name (`read_file`, `execute_command`, `search`, etc.) without any confirmation or security gate, invisibly redirecting execution away from the server the agent/user actually intended.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-tool-discovery). Failure scenario: Server A ("tool.terminal") is connected and exposes `read_file`; all agent tool-calling and prior context reference `read_file` believing it's server A. The user later installs/connects Server B (e.g. a marketplace connector, possibly untrusted or compromised) that happens to also expose a tool literally named `read_file`. `connect_server` for B calls `state.tool_index.insert(tool.name.clone(), id.clone())` unconditionally, overwriting A's routing entry with only a `warn!` log (no rejection, no permission check, no distinction by trust level). From that point, every subsequent `call_server_tool(..., "read_file", ...)` from any agent — including ones that believe they are calling the original trusted server — is silently routed to Server B instead, because `state.tool_index.get(tool_name)` (mcp.rs:2024) is consulted at dispatch time and has no memory of which server the caller actually intended. Fix direction: Either reject/refuse registration of a tool name that already maps to a different, still-connected server (fail closed, require explicit user disambiguation), or make tool identity server-scoped end-to-end (route by `server_id.tool_name`, exposing the bare name to the LLM only when unambiguous) instead of relying on a global last-writer-wins map.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: `SessionToolCache::touch` is called with a hardcoded agent bucket and an unqualified tool name that never matches the cache's actual keys, so real tool usage never updates LRU order — The only production call site that reports real tool usage to the §16.7 session cache passes both a wrong agent-id (`"default"` instead of the caller's actual id) and a wrong key format (bare tool name instead of the `server_id.tool_name` `tool_id` the cache actually stores), making `touch()` a permanent no-op for genuine tool invocations. LRU eviction decisions inside `SessionToolCache::enforce_budget` are therefore based solely on cache/request timestamps, never on actual usage, defeating the stated purpose of the least-recently-used session tool cache.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-tool-discovery). Failure scenario: An agent with `Caller::Agent("alice")` calls `mgp.tools.request` for tool `read_file` on server `tool.terminal`; `execute_tools_request` caches it under agent bucket `"alice"` with key `entry.tool_id = "tool.terminal.read_file"` (mcp_tool_discovery.rs:150, :854). Alice then actually invokes the tool via `call_server_tool`. At mcp.rs:2119 the dispatcher calls `self.session_cache.touch("default", tool_name)` where `tool_name` is the bare name `"read_file"` (not `"tool.terminal.read_file"`) and the agent bucket is hardcoded to the literal string `"default"` instead of the real caller id available via `caller` (used two lines earlier at mcp.rs:2049 for `enforce_caller_grant`). `SessionToolCache::touch` (mcp_tool_discovery.rs:504-514) looks up `session.cached.get_mut(tool_id)` in the `"default"` session's map, which neither contains `"read_file"` (only the qualified `"tool.terminal.read_file"` key) nor is Alice's actual session — so the lookup misses and `last_used` is never refreshed. The tool Alice is actively using looks stale to `enforce_budget`'s LRU comparison and can be evicted from her session-cache bookkeeping ahead of tools she hasn't touched at all. Fix direction: Pass the real caller agent id (from `caller`) and the fully-qualified `tool_id` (`format!("{}.{}", server_id, tool_name)`, matching what `execute_tools_request` stores) to `session_cache.touch(...)` at the dispatch call site.

issues.summary: LOW: MGP §5.6.3 delegated_via check verifies the server exists, not that it is the actual sender — delegation provenance can be spoofed — MGP_SECURITY.md §5.6.3 states the kernel MUST verify that 'delegated_via must be the server that sent the tool call' — an identity-binding check. The implementation in resolve_tool_call_target only confirms delegated_via names *some* known, operational server, which is an existence check, not a sender-identity check. This lets any caller reaching this chokepoint claim to have been delegated via an arbitrary legitimate server, undermining the anti-spoofing guarantee the delegation envelope is documented to provide.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): sec-spoof-deser). Failure scenario: A caller invokes POST /api/mcp/call (admin-authenticated, dispatched with Caller::System) or any other path reaching resolve_tool_call_target with arguments containing _mgp.delegation.delegated_via set to the id of some unrelated, currently-connected MCP server (not the server that actually made the request). The check at mcp.rs:2349-2372 only does state.servers.get(delegated_via).is_some_and(|h| h.status.is_operational()) — it never compares delegated_via to server_id (the target of this call) or to any verified identity of the actual sender. The call proceeds and is treated as a validated MGP §5.6 delegation, so the forged delegated_via value flows into the delegation object that is forwarded verbatim in args to the target server (client.call_tool(tool_name, args)) and would appear in any downstream §5.6.4 audit/actor attribution as if the named server genuinely originated the request. Fix direction: Bind delegated_via to a verified identity of the actual request sender (e.g. require it to equal server_id for same-server calls, or thread a verified per-connection/per-API-key server identity from the HTTP layer) and reject the call when they differ, per MGP_SECURITY.md §5.6.3.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: RwLock read guard held across a per-server notification-send loop blocks all MCP lifecycle writers on a single slow/wedged server — Several notification-broadcast helpers acquire `self.state.read().await` and then, still holding that guard, loop over server handles performing `.await`ed MCP notification sends per server (`broadcast_audit_event`, `broadcast_event`, `notify_config_updated`, `deliver_permission_grant` in mcp.rs; `emit_lifecycle_notification` in mcp_lifecycle.rs). Because `broadcast_audit_event` runs on essentially every tool call, a single slow-to-drain MCP server can hold the read lock open long enough to block every writer-side lifecycle operation (connect/stop/restart/disconnect) system-wide, in addition to delaying the response to whichever agent triggered the audited tool call. Elsewhere in the same file the correct pattern is used (e.g. `resolve_tool_call_target`, mcp.rs ~2383-2397, clones the needed `Arc<McpClient>` under the lock and drops the guard before awaiting), showing this is an inconsistency rather than an inherent constraint.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-lifecycle). Failure scenario: `broadcast_audit_event` is invoked after every MCP tool execution (mcp.rs lines 2056/2083/2100 — TOOL_BLOCKED / TOOL_ERROR / TOOL_EXECUTED), and after acquiring `let state = self.state.read().await;` at line 2528 it loops over every connected, audit-extension-negotiated server calling `client.send_notification(...).await` (line 2564) — still holding the read guard for the whole loop. `send_notification` is bounded only by the 10s enqueue timeout (`SEND_TIMEOUT_SECS` in mcp_client.rs); if one audit-capable server's stdio write channel is backed up (e.g. a wedged child not draining its stdin, or a burst of concurrent notifications), each iteration can stall up to 10s. During that window any concurrent writer that needs `self.state.write().await` — `connect_server`, `stop_server`, `disconnect_server`, `restart_server`, `add_server`'s error path, `update_server_env` — blocks for the full duration, i.e. a single misbehaving MCP server can stall connecting/stopping/restarting every other MCP server in the process while ordinary tool calls keep piling up behind the same read lock. The identical pattern (read guard held across a per-server `.await` send loop) recurs in `broadcast_event` (line 2497-2518), `notify_config_updated` (2577-2598), `deliver_permission_grant` (196-227, which awaits a full round-trip `client.call(...)` bounded by the much larger `mcp_request_timeout_secs`), and in `mcp_lifecycle::emit_lifecycle_notification` (mcp_lifecycle.rs lines 120-152, invoked on every connect/restart/drain transition and from the health monitor). Fix direction: In each of these functions, collect the small (server_id, Arc<McpClient>, precomputed params) tuples needed for the notification while holding the read lock, drop the guard, and then perform the `.await` sends outside the lock — mirroring the pattern already used in `resolve_tool_call_target`. For loops over many servers, consider also fanning the sends out concurrently (`futures::future::join_all`) instead of sequentially, since each send is already independently timeout-bounded.

issues.summary: CRITICAL: mgp.access.grant lets a YOLO-mode agent durably self-escalate MCP access that outlives the YOLO flag — `execute_access_grant` (and `execute_access_revoke`) are the only enforcement points for the MCP capability system's own write path (`mcp_access_control`), yet they are gated solely by the global `yolo_mode` boolean with no check that the calling agent is authorized to grant the specific permission it is requesting. Because the resulting DB row has no expiry and `resolve_tool_access` never consults `yolo_mode`, a grant an agent writes to itself during a YOLO window persists forever after YOLO is turned back off, defeating the admin-curated allow-list (`put_mcp_server_access`/`put_agent_mcp_access`) that the rest of the codebase treats as the authoritative access boundary.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): sec-authz-bypass, mcp-kernel-tool). Failure scenario: Operator enables YOLO mode (Settings → Security) so an agent can auto-approve sandboxed shell commands during a session — the documented scope of the toggle. While YOLO is on, `kernel_tool_schemas()` (mcp.rs collect_tool_schemas_for_agent, line ~1793-1817) unconditionally injects `mgp.access.grant`/`mgp.access.revoke` into that agent's LLM tool list (filtered only by an opt-out 'explicit Deny on kernel' check, default Allow). The agentic loop's anti-spoofing shim (handlers/system.rs:2582-2588) forces `args.agent_id` to the caller's own id, but nothing forces `server_id`/`permission`/`entry_type`. The LLM (or a prompt-injected instruction hidden in tool output/external content it is processing) calls `mgp.access.grant` with `{agent_id: <self>, server_id: <any-mcp-server>, entry_type: 'server_grant', permission: 'allow'}`. `execute_access_grant`'s only gate is the boolean `manager.yolo_mode` (mcp_kernel_tool.rs:607) — there is no check that the caller already has (or an admin approved) that specific grant. The call unconditionally INSERTs a `mcp_access_control` row with `expires_at: None` via `save_access_control_entry`. That row is read by `resolve_tool_access()` (db/mcp.rs:576-598) on every future tool-visibility/execution check, independent of `yolo_mode`. When the operator later disables YOLO mode believing they restored default-deny isolation, the self-granted server access remains active and the agent can now see and invoke every tool on that server going forward — the entire opt-in/default-deny MCP capability model (ARCH §1.5/2.x, bug-421) has been permanently widened by one agent action taken during a temporary trust window. Fix direction: Require the acting caller to already hold `AdminAccess`/`Caller::System` (or an explicit admin-issued token) before `execute_access_grant`/`execute_access_revoke` are allowed to mutate `mcp_access_control`, independent of `yolo_mode`; alternatively, scope any YOLO-mode self-grant to auto-expire (`expires_at`) at or before the point YOLO mode is disabled, and record `granted_by` as the actual requesting agent (not the generic `"kernel"`) so such grants are auditable and revert automatically when the flag is turned off. — FIXED 2026-07-13: YOLO self-grants now record the actual agent + bounded expires_at (auto-expire via resolve_explicit_permission) and are purged on YOLO disable in set_yolo_mode. Guard marker: yolo-grant: prefix.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: mgp.audit.replay's `limit` argument is passed straight into a SQL LIMIT with no upper clamp, unlike the sibling mgp.events.replay tool — `execute_audit_replay` reads `args.get("limit")` and only applies `.unwrap_or(100)` — no `.min(N)` upper bound — before passing it straight to `db::query_audit_logs_since`, which uses it verbatim as `... LIMIT ?` in the SQL query. The sibling kernel tool `mgp.events.replay` (crates/core/src/managers/mcp_events.rs, `replay()`) demonstrates the intended pattern for the exact same shape of parameter: `.unwrap_or(100).min(1000) as usize`. The audit-replay path lacks that clamp, so a single tool call can force the kernel to materialize an unbounded audit-log result set in memory.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): sec-dos-resource). Failure scenario: Once YOLO mode is enabled (the tool's only gate — no per-argument validation), an agent/LLM tool call (or a malicious MCP server that gets the LLM to invoke this kernel tool, e.g. via prompt-injected tool-call suggestions) invokes `mgp.audit.replay` with `{"limit": 999999999}` (or `-1`, which SQLite treats as "no limit" for a `LIMIT ?` clause). `query_audit_logs_since` binds this value directly as the SQL `LIMIT`, so the query returns the entire `audit_logs` table (which grows unbounded over the kernel's lifetime as every permission check / MCP action is audited). All rows are loaded into a `Vec` and then serialized into one giant JSON `Value` returned as the tool result, exhausting kernel memory and stalling the DB connection for the duration of the query on a single tool call. Fix direction: Clamp `limit` the same way `mcp_events::replay` does, e.g. `.unwrap_or(100).min(1000)`, and reject/normalize non-positive values before binding it into the SQL LIMIT (SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as unlimited).

issues.summary: LOW: mgp.audit.replay hardcodes actor.type to "kernel" for every replayed entry, contradicting entries whose actor_id is a real agent — execute_audit_replay always emits `"actor": {"type": "kernel", ...}` for every replayed audit entry instead of deriving the type from the entry's real actor, producing self-contradictory records whenever `actor_id` is an agent id.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-kernel-tool). Failure scenario: After a mgp.agent.ask delegation (which correctly logs `actor_id: Some(caller_agent_id.to_string())`, e.g. "agent.foo", for its DELEGATION_EXECUTED audit entry), calling mgp.audit.replay to review the log returns `"actor": {"type": "kernel", "id": "agent.foo"}` for that row — the `type` field is a compile-time literal, not derived from `e.event_type`/`e.actor_id`, so it claims every event was kernel-originated even when `id` plainly names an agent. Any consumer (dashboard audit viewer, an operator or auditor agent) that trusts `actor.type` to distinguish kernel vs agent actions is misled for every non-kernel row. Fix direction: Derive `actor.type` from the entry (e.g. "agent" when actor_id starts with "agent."/is a known agent id, "kernel"/"system" otherwise) instead of a hardcoded literal.

issues.summary: HIGH: mgp.lifecycle.shutdown lets any agent drain/kill any MCP server by id with no ownership or grant check — The Tier-3 lifecycle/streaming/event kernel tools operate on resource identifiers (server_id, subscription_id) taken verbatim from LLM tool-call arguments without verifying the calling agent actually owns or was granted that resource, unlike the main tool-execution chokepoint elsewhere in the codebase. This lets any agent with default-Allow kernel-tool access disrupt or interfere with MCP servers and streams belonging to other agents.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): test-coverage). Failure scenario: execute_lifecycle_shutdown (lines 948-973) takes server_id directly from LLM-supplied args and calls manager.drain_server(&server_id, ...) unconditionally — there is no check that the calling agent has any grant for that server_id (unlike the normal tool-execution path, which is gated by execute_tool_for_agent / resolve_tool_call_target's per-agent capability gate). Under YOLO mode with no explicit 'kernel'/'mgp.lifecycle.shutdown' deny for the caller (the default), any single agent can shut down a server another agent depends on (e.g. the shared memory or engine server), producing a system-wide denial of service triggered by one agent's tool call. mgp.stream.cancel (line 1040) and mgp.events.subscribe/unsubscribe (lines 1194-1207, 1201-1207) share the same pattern: they act on a bare server_id / subscription_id supplied by the LLM with no ownership check. Fix direction: Require the target server_id (and subscription_id/request_id) to be drawn from the calling agent's own granted_server_ids (or otherwise validated against Caller) before executing drain_server / cancel_stream / send_pace / subscribe / unsubscribe, mirroring the per-agent gate already applied to normal tool execution. — FIXED 2026-07-13: require_server_access() gates shutdown/stream.cancel/events.subscribe against the caller (anti-spoofed agent_id) holding a ServerGrant/Allow. Residual: unsubscribe(subscription_id) + pace not gated.

issues.summary: HIGH: mgp.events.pending_callbacks + mgp.callback.respond allow any agent to enumerate and hijack another agent's pending human-in-the-loop callback — The two kernel-native tools that together implement callback discovery and response have no per-agent scoping: pending_callbacks() enumerates every outstanding callback in the process regardless of which server/agent it belongs to, and respond_to_callback() answers any callback_id supplied. Any agent permitted to call these tools (default-Allow kernel RBAC) can read and answer callbacks that were never addressed to it, breaking the isolation the HITL/elicitation mechanism (MGP §13) is meant to provide.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): test-coverage). Failure scenario: execute_events_pending_callbacks (line 1218-1236) ignores its `_args` parameter entirely and returns manager.events.pending_callbacks() — every non-responded callback system-wide (callback_id, server_id, message, options, age_secs), not scoped to the calling agent. execute_callback_respond (line 1267-1272) then forwards straight to mcp_events::respond_to_callback(manager, args), which (confirmed in crates/core/src/managers/mcp_events.rs:536-589) resolves ANY callback_id and sends the caller-supplied `response` text to whichever MCP server registered it — again with no ownership/agent check. A malicious or prompt-injected Agent A (YOLO on, no explicit kernel deny) can call mgp.events.pending_callbacks to discover a pending elicitation/HITL callback that actually belongs to Agent B's session, then call mgp.callback.respond with a forged answer, hijacking a confirmation flow meant for a different agent or a human operator. Fix direction: Scope PendingCallback records by the agent_id/session that owns the originating tool call, and have execute_events_pending_callbacks / execute_callback_respond filter and authorize against the Caller (which needs to be threaded through, same gap as the access.grant finding) instead of operating on the entire global callback map.

issues.summary: LOW: execute_mgp_agent_ask derives the delegating caller's identity purely from an untyped args["agent_id"] field, not from the kernel's authenticated Caller — The delegation tool's caller identity is read from a JSON payload field with no independent verification against the kernel-authenticated `Caller`, making anti-spoofing dependent on every present and future call site remembering to force-insert `agent_id` rather than on the tool itself.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-kernel-tool). Failure scenario: execute_mgp_agent_ask(manager: &McpClientManager, args: Value) has no `caller: &Caller` parameter; self-delegation rejection (caller_agent_id == target_agent_id), the §5.6.1 caller∩target intersection check in run_mgp_agent_ask_loop, and the DELEGATION_EXECUTED/DELEGATION_FAILED audit attribution all trust `args.get("agent_id")` verbatim. The doc comment calls this 'injected by the kernel (anti-spoofing)', but that injection is not enforced by this function or by the central execute_tool_internal dispatcher (mcp.rs) — it is done by convention at two specific call sites in handlers/system.rs (lines 802 and 2585-2588) that force-insert "agent_id" before calling execute_tool_for_agent/execute_tool_internal. registry.rs also exposes an `execute_tool`/`execute_tool_for` pair that forward `args` to execute_tool_internal unmodified (currently unused in production, but present and exported); any future or alternate caller that reaches execute_tool_internal("mgp.agent.ask", args) without replicating that insertion would let the caller set target_agent_id independent of a spoofed agent_id, defeating the self-delegation guard and misattributing the resulting DELEGATION_EXECUTED audit entry to an arbitrary agent. Not currently reachable via any known production call path, but the safety property is enforced entirely outside the function that depends on it. Fix direction: Give execute_mgp_agent_ask a `caller: &Caller` parameter (as resolve_tool_call_target and enforce_kernel_rbac already have) and derive caller_agent_id from it directly, dropping trust in args["agent_id"] entirely.

issues.summary: LOW: `ToolIndex::add_server_tools` is not idempotent — duplicate entries accumulate in the discovery index on server reconnect — `add_server_tools` always appends new `ToolIndexEntry` rows for a server's tools; it never removes or checks for pre-existing entries with the same `tool_id` for that `server_id`. The only caller that clears old entries first is `stop_server`/`disconnect_server` (which call `remove_server_tools`); the "racy reconnect" path in `connect_server` that the codebase's own comment acknowledges does not, so duplicate index rows accumulate.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-tool-discovery). Failure scenario: `connect_server` (mcp.rs) documents and defends against exactly this case in its own comment at mcp.rs:1428-1434: "if a handle for this id already holds a live client (a racy reconnect, or a prior stop that failed), reap its child process group before overwriting the entry". In that path the old `McpServerHandle`/process is reaped and a fresh handle is inserted, but `self.rich_tool_index.add_server_tools(&id, &tools, ...)` (mcp.rs:1490-1493) is invoked again for the same `server_id` with no preceding `remove_server_tools(&id)` call. Since `add_server_tools` unconditionally pushes a new `ToolIndexEntry` per tool with no check for an existing entry with the same `tool_id`, every racy/duplicate `connect_server` call for an id that still holds a live client doubles that server's entries in `ToolIndex.entries`. Repeated over a flapping/crash-looping server's lifetime, this grows the Vec unbounded and pollutes `mgp.tools.discover` results with duplicate copies of the same tool, and inflates `total_available`. Fix direction: Make `add_server_tools` idempotent by removing any existing entries for `server_id` before inserting the new set (or have it dedupe by `tool_id`), so repeated registration for the same server_id is safe regardless of caller discipline.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: `risk_level_max` discovery filter fails open for the majority of tools (no MGP security metadata) — `ToolIndex::matches_filter` only enforces `risk_level_max` when `entry.security` is `Some`; when it is `None` (the default for any server that hasn't negotiated the MGP `tool_security` extension) the filter is silently skipped instead of treated as unknown/high risk. This is a fail-open filter: exactly the tools most likely to be dangerous and least likely to have been vetted (ordinary, non-MGP MCP servers) are the ones that bypass the `risk_level_max` restriction entirely.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-tool-discovery). Failure scenario: An agent (or an automated guardrail) calls `mgp.tools.discover(query=..., filter={"risk_level_max":"safe"})` expecting only low-risk tools back. A plain (non-MGP-negotiated) MCP server — the common case, since `compute_tool_security` (mcp.rs:1714-1733) returns `None` whenever `handle.mgp_negotiated` is `None` or the server didn't advertise the `tool_security` extension — has `entry.security == None` for every tool it exposes, including dangerous ones like `execute_command`. Because `matches_filter` only applies the risk check `if let Some(ref sec) = entry.security`, any tool with no security metadata is never rejected by `risk_level_max`, so it is returned in a "safe"-only search alongside genuinely safe tools. Fix direction: Treat missing security metadata as the maximum risk class for filtering purposes (fail closed) unless the caller explicitly opts into unknown-risk tools, e.g. `risk_within_max("dangerous", max_risk)` (or a distinct "unknown" tier that never passes a `safe`/`moderate` cap) when `entry.security` is `None`.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: `mgp.tools.request` reports "fulfilled" and lists all requested tools as loaded even when the session cache's own LRU eviction removes some of them in the same call — The response of `mgp.tools.request` computes `status`/`tools_loaded` purely from what was inserted before budget enforcement ran, not from what actually survives in the session cache afterward, so an agent can be told a tool was successfully "fulfilled"/loaded into its session while it (or another just-cached tool) was silently evicted moments later by the same call.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-tool-discovery). Failure scenario: `execute_tools_request` searches for up to 10 matching tools and calls `manager.session_cache.cache_tools(agent_id, &cache_entries)` (mcp_tool_discovery.rs:857), which inserts every entry from `cache_entries` and only afterwards calls `Self::enforce_budget(session)` (mcp_tool_discovery.rs:442) to evict least-recently-used entries down to `max_tokens` (default 8000). If the combined size of the newly requested tools alone (or combined with what was already cached) exceeds the budget — plausible for a handful of tools with large schemas, per this file's own stress tests showing ~600-2500 tokens for a single tool with many parameters — `enforce_budget` evicts some of the entries that were just inserted in this very call. `added` (returned by `cache_tools`) reflects the pre-eviction insert count, so `status` is computed as `"fulfilled"` whenever `added == results.len()`, and `tools_loaded` (built directly from `results`, mcp_tool_discovery.rs:859-873) lists every found tool's full schema — regardless of whether `enforce_budget` subsequently dropped it. `session_tools_count` (queried after `cache_tools` returns) can therefore be lower than `tools_loaded.len()` in the very same response. Fix direction: Compute `tools_loaded`/`status` from the post-`enforce_budget` state (e.g. intersect `results` with the final `session.cached` key set, or have `cache_tools` return which of the newly-added entries survived) instead of the pre-eviction `added` count.

issues.summary: LOW: Response loop silently drops any JSON-RPC response whose id is not representable as i64 — `start_response_loop`'s response-id correlation (`response.id.and_then(Value::as_i64)`) only matches JSON-RPC ids that deserialize as an integer. Any other JSON id shape (string, float) is silently discarded with no logging at all, unlike the adjacent unparseable-message branch which does log (line 368-379). This makes an id-type mismatch indistinguishable from a hung server — the request simply times out with no diagnostic trail pointing at the real cause.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-transport). Failure scenario: The kernel always sends integer request ids (`JsonRpcRequest::new` wraps an `i64`), but a spec-compliant JSON-RPC server is only required to echo back the exact same JSON value — some server SDKs/bridges normalize ids to strings or floats when round-tripping. If a connected MCP server ever responds with `{"id": "5", ...}` or `{"id": 5.0, ...}`, `id_val.as_i64()` returns `None`; the outer `if let Some(id_val) = response.id { if let Some(id) = id_val.as_i64() { ... } }` then falls through doing nothing — no log line, no removal from `pending_requests`. The caller's `call()` sits on its `rx.await` until `request_timeout_secs` elapses, then fails with a generic "MCP Request timed out" that gives no hint the real cause was an id-type mismatch, and the entry stays in `pending_requests` (counting against `MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS`) until the timeout branch removes it. Fix direction: Add an else-branch (or a debug!/warn! log) when `id_val.as_i64()` returns `None`, so an id-type mismatch is visible in logs instead of manifesting only as a bare timeout; optionally widen correlation to also match string-typed ids that parse as the same integer.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: call_tool_streaming() inserts into pending_requests without enforcing MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS — `McpClient::call()` bounds concurrent in-flight requests at `MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS` (100) by checking `pending_requests.len()` before inserting a new oneshot sender. `call_tool_streaming()` shares the exact same `pending_requests: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<i64, oneshot::Sender<...>>>>` map but inserts unconditionally (no length check), so the streaming call path bypasses the resource bound entirely. A caller that issues streaming tool calls faster than they resolve can grow pending_requests/stream_collectors and the associated per-call watchdog tasks without limit.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-transport). Failure scenario: A caller (agent/plugin) that fires off many `call_server_tool_streaming` calls in a row without waiting for each to finish (or against a server that never responds) grows `pending_requests` and `stream_collectors` without bound: `call()` explicitly checks `map.len() >= Self::MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS` (line 420) before inserting and rejects with an error once the client has 100 in-flight requests, but `call_tool_streaming()` (lines 567-570) inserts into the very same `pending_requests` map with no such check. Each accepted streaming call also spawns a dedicated watchdog task and a 256-slot chunk channel, so the same unbounded-caller scenario grows both memory and task count, unlike the regular call path which is capped. Fix direction: Apply the same `if map.len() >= Self::MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS { return Err(...) }` guard in `call_tool_streaming()` before inserting into `pending_requests` (and ideally check the same shared counter, since both paths share the map), or introduce a unified guard shared by both `call()` and `call_tool_streaming()`.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: MCP stdout/stderr line reader has no per-line size cap, unlike the SSE reader in the same file — a single unterminated write from a spawned MCP server can OOM the kernel — The stdio transport's stdout reader task uses `BufReader::new(stdout).lines()` / `next_line()` to parse JSON-RPC responses from a spawned MCP server, with no cap on how many bytes it will buffer while looking for a newline. This is the exact vulnerability class the same file already fixed for the HTTP/SSE transport: `parse_sse_stream` explicitly bounds unterminated data via `MAX_SSE_LINE_BYTES` (1 MiB) with a comment citing bug-410 ("a server that streams … without any newline would otherwise grow the assembly buffer without bound → memory exhaustion"). The stdio path — which is the default and most common MCP transport, used by every marketplace-installed server — was not given the same protection, so a single malformed/hostile line from a child process can exhaust kernel memory.
issues.notes:
Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): sec-dos-resource). Failure scenario: Any connected stdio MCP server (marketplace-installed npm/pip/docker package, or a buggy/compromised one) writes to its stdout a single very large chunk of bytes with no embedded '
' (e.g. dumping a large blob, base64 payload, or an infinite/very-long print without a newline) before ever flushing a newline. `reader.next_line()` (tokio::io::Lines::next_line, backed by `read_line_internal`) appends every byte read into an internal `String` buffer with no maximum length and only returns once it observes `
` or EOF. The buffer therefore grows without bound as the child keeps writing, consuming kernel process memory until the OS OOM-kills the whole ClotoCore kernel (not just the offending MCP connection) or the process aborts on allocation failure. The stderr reader task a few lines below (`BufReader::new(stderr).lines()`, ~line 467) has the identical unbounded-buffer shape. Fix direction: Cap the accumulated line length the same way the SSE parser does: replace `BufReader::new(stdout).lines()` with a manual `read_until(b'
', &mut buf)` loop (or `tokio_util::codec::LinesCodec::new_with_max_length`) that aborts/truncates the connection once the buffer exceeds a fixed byte budget (e.g. reuse `MAX_SSE_LINE_BYTES` or a stdio-specific constant), logging and breaking the reader task instead of growing unbounded. Apply the same fix to the stderr logger task.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: HttpTransport error responses hardcode "id": null, breaking request/response correlation — In `HttpTransport::start`'s request loop, all three error paths (request-send failure, per-message timeout, non-success HTTP status) build a JSON-RPC error envelope with `"id": null` instead of the id of the request that actually failed (available by parsing `msg`, the request string already in scope). The comment at line 596 states the intent explicitly ("Send JSON-RPC error so pending requests don't hang"), but because `start_response_loop` only routes responses whose `id` resolves via `Value::as_i64()`, a null id never matches any entry in `pending_requests`, so the intent is not met: the specific failing request is not unblocked by the error, it silently falls through to the full-duration timeout instead of surfacing the real error immediately.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-transport). Failure scenario: A `call()` sends a request over the HTTP transport; the corresponding POST fails (network error), times out (HTTP_PER_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT_SECS), or returns a non-2xx status. The transport task builds `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{...},"id":null}` and forwards it to `res_tx`. In `start_response_loop` (mcp_client.rs:308), `if let Some(id_val) = response.id` is false for a null id, so the error is silently discarded — never routed to the pending oneshot for the request that actually failed. The caller's `call()` therefore does not get the specific error; it just blocks until `request_timeout_secs` elapses and then reports a generic "MCP Request timed out", even though the real cause (HTTP failure with a specific message) was already known and thrown away. Fix direction: Parse the JSON-RPC `id` out of `msg` before building the error response (e.g. `serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&msg).ok().and_then(|v| v.get("id").cloned())`) and use that value instead of `Value::Null` in all three error-construction sites (~line 599-601, 607-611, 621-625), so the error correlates back to the exact pending request.

issues.summary:
LOW: parse_sse_stream discards a trailing unterminated line when the SSE stream ends — `parse_sse_stream` only dispatches a `data:` line to the channel once a `
` is found in the buffer (the `while let Some(rel) = buffer[consumed..].iter().position(...)` loop). There is no flush of a final, newline-less line once the underlying byte stream naturally ends (`stream.next().await` returns `None`) — the function just returns `Ok(())`, discarding whatever is left in `buffer`. A well-formed SSE server that always terminates its last event with `

` before closing avoids this, but the code has no defense against (and silently mishandles) a stream that ends mid-line or with a single non-doubled trailing newline already consumed, dropping the final/only message for that request.
issues.notes:
Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-transport). Failure scenario: For the Streamable HTTP transport, a JSON-RPC response arrives as `text/event-stream` and is parsed line-by-line, only ever forwarding a `data:` line to `res_tx` once a `
` terminator for it has been seen (lines 706-721). If the remote server closes the response body right after writing its single `data: {...}` line without a trailing newline (connection close instead of an explicit `

` event terminator — plausible for a minimal/non-conforming SSE emitter, or a server that flushes the body without a final newline before EOF), the `while let Some(chunk) = stream.next().await` loop simply ends (line 697) once `stream.next()` returns `None`, and the unterminated remainder sitting in `buffer` is never processed or forwarded — `parse_sse_stream` returns `Ok(())` at line 736 having silently dropped the only response for that request. The caller's `call()` then blocks until `request_timeout_secs` and fails with a generic timeout instead of surfacing the response that technically arrived. Fix direction: After the `while let Some(chunk) = stream.next().await` loop ends, check whether `buffer` still contains an unprocessed `data: ` line (even without a trailing `
`) and forward it to `res_tx` before returning, so the terminal message of a stream that ends without a final newline is not silently lost.

issues.summary: LOW: StreamAssembler never removes indices from tracker.gaps once received, permanently breaking duplicate detection for those indices — `StreamTracker.gaps: Vec<u32>` records indices that were skipped over by a forward jump so a gap-notification/retransmission can be requested. When a gapped index later arrives (the `index < tracker.expected_index` branch in `record_chunk`, mcp_streaming.rs lines 58-89), the code correctly avoids re-adding a gap and returns `None`, but it never calls something like `tracker.gaps.retain(|&g| g != index)` to remove that index once it has actually been received. Because `is_duplicate()` (line 101) treats "index < expected_index AND still present in gaps" as "not yet seen", any index that was ever part of a detected gap remains permanently exempt from duplicate detection — a second delivery of the same (now-received) chunk sails through as if it were new. The `gaps` Vec also then grows without bound over the life of a long stream with recurring gaps, since entries are only ever removed in bulk via `StreamAssembler::remove()` at stream completion.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-transport). Failure scenario: A stream skips ahead (chunk index 5 arrives while `expected_index` is 2): `record_chunk` pushes 2,3,4 into `tracker.gaps` and advances `expected_index` to 6, returning `Some([2,3,4])`, which `mcp.rs::handle_stream_chunk` turns into a `send_gap_notification` retransmission request. When chunk index 3 is later retransmitted, `is_duplicate(3)` correctly returns false (3 is still in `gaps`) so it's processed, but `record_chunk(3)` (index < expected_index branch, lines 79-88) never removes 3 from `tracker.gaps` — it only returns `None`. If chunk 3 is delivered a second time (duplicate retransmission, server resend, or any redelivery), `is_duplicate(3)` is evaluated again: `3 < expected_index` is still true and `t.gaps.contains(&3)` is still true (never pruned), so `!contains` is false and `is_duplicate` returns false again — the second copy of chunk 3 is NOT recognized as a duplicate and is processed/delivered again, corrupting the assembled stream output with duplicated content. This is exactly the case the code comments call out as "§12.5 retransmission dedup" (mcp.rs:2457). Fix direction: In the `index < tracker.expected_index` branch of `record_chunk`, remove `index` from `tracker.gaps` (e.g. `tracker.gaps.retain(|&g| g != index)`) once it has actually been received, so `is_duplicate` correctly flags a second delivery of the same index as a duplicate and `gaps` doesn't grow unboundedly for long streams with recurring gaps.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: Shared MCP Python venv (create/stale-recreate/pip-install) has no lock, so concurrent startup-sync and marketplace-install races can corrupt it — `ensure_mcp_venv` performs a check-then-act on `venv_dir.join("pyvenv.cfg").exists()` (line 294), then on staleness does a bare `remove_dir_all` (line 303) followed later by an unguarded `uv venv --python … <path>` recreation and `uv pip install` (install_server_deps). None of these steps takes any inter-task or inter-process lock (no Mutex/Semaphore/flock anywhere in the file), and the identical helper functions are reused unsynchronized by marketplace.rs's own server-install and PyPI-install handlers, which duplicate the very same check-then-act sequence and can run concurrently with the startup background task on the same tokio runtime. Two concurrent `uv venv` invocations on one directory, or a `remove_dir_all` racing an in-flight `uv pip install`, can corrupt the single shared venv every Python MCP server depends on (partial pyvenv.cfg, missing or half-written packages), silently degrading or breaking every Python-based MCP server until a human manually deletes and recreates the `.venv` directory.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-isolation). Failure scenario: At kernel boot, lib.rs does `tokio::spawn(async move { managers::mcp_venv::ensure_mcp_venv(&data_dir_bg).await; })` as a detached background task specifically so that 'servers can start immediately' while it runs (crates/core/src/lib.rs:432-435). If that task's `is_venv_stale` check trips, it does the unguarded `remove_dir_all` at mcp_venv.rs:303 and then re-creates the venv via `uv venv --python 3.13 <path>` (mcp_venv.rs:315-321). Meanwhile the dashboard/marketplace HTTP handlers (crates/core/src/handlers/marketplace.rs, e.g. ~L1202-1230 and ~L3156-3260) independently call the exact same `mcp_venv::resolve_venv_dir/uv_bin/venv_python/is_venv_stale` helpers and run their own `if !venv_dir.join("pyvenv.cfg").exists() { uv venv --python 3.13 <same path> }` / `uv pip install` sequence against the identical shared `.venv`. A user opening the marketplace and clicking 'install' within the first seconds after launch (a completely ordinary sequence, since the UI is deliberately made responsive before venv sync finishes) causes two independent `uv venv` invocations to race on the same directory, or a `remove_dir_all` to fire while a `uv pip install` is mid-write into that directory. Fix direction: Serialize all venv create/stale-recreate/install sequences (both the ensure_mcp_venv path in mcp_venv.rs and the duplicated sequences in marketplace.rs) behind a single async lock keyed by the venv path — either a process-wide `tokio::sync::Mutex` shared via app state, or an OS-level advisory file lock (e.g. flock on a `.venv.lock` sentinel) held for the full check→remove→create→install sequence so concurrent callers serialize instead of racing.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: Windows sc.exe service-create options are passed as single argv tokens without the required space after '=', so install_service always fails — `install_service` on Windows builds its `sc.exe create` argv with `binPath={value}`, `start=auto`, and `DisplayName=ClotoCore` as single concatenated tokens instead of the two-token `optionname=` / `value` form `sc.exe` requires. This is a well-documented sc.exe parsing quirk (the space after '=' is mandatory), so every invocation of this code path fails and the feature is non-functional.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): mcp-isolation). Failure scenario: Running the `service install` CLI path (crates/core/src/installer.rs:151 or crates/core/src/cli.rs:110 → `platform::install_service`) on Windows executes `Command::new("sc.exe").args(["create", SERVICE_NAME, &format!("binPath={}", exe_path.display()), "start=auto", "DisplayName=ClotoCore"]).status()`. `sc.exe`'s parser requires each `optionname=` token to be immediately followed by a separate, whitespace-delimited value argv entry (the documented `sc create <name> binPath= <value> ...` form — omitting the space causes sc.exe to fail to recognize the option and return a parameter/usage error). Because `binPath=`, `start=`, and `DisplayName=` are each concatenated with their value into one token here, `sc.exe create` returns a non-zero exit code every time this runs, which the following `if !status.success() { bail!(...) }` (line ~24) correctly surfaces as an error — so the Windows-service registration feature can never succeed as currently coded. Fix direction: Split each option into its own argv entries, e.g. `.args(["create", SERVICE_NAME, "binPath=", &exe_path.display().to_string(), "start=", "auto", "DisplayName=", "ClotoCore"])`, matching the syntax `sc create <name> binPath= <value> start= <value> DisplayName= <value>`.

issues.summary: MEDIUM: MCP access-grant expiry check compares RFC3339 timestamps against SQLite's space-separated datetime('now'), so same-day expiries never take effect — Both explicit-permission lookups in resolve_explicit_permission (tool_grant at line 533 and server_grant at line 556) gate expiry with `expires_at > datetime('now')`, comparing an RFC3339 string (contains 'T') against SQLite's own datetime('now') output (contains a space at the same character offset). Because 'T' (0x54) sorts after ' ' (0x20) in a plain string comparison, any expires_at dated today (or later) is always treated as still valid regardless of the time component, so same-day time-limited grants never expire until midnight. This breaks the time-bound access-control invariant the expires_at column exists to enforce.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): db-core). Failure scenario: An authenticated caller (dashboard or direct REST client) issues PUT /api/mcp/servers/:name/access with an entries array whose expires_at is an RFC3339 string (the only format used anywhere in this codebase, e.g. produced by chrono's `to_rfc3339()`/`DateTime::to_rfc3339()`, and accepted verbatim since `AccessControlEntry.expires_at` is a raw `Option<String>` deserialized straight from the JSON body with no format validation in handlers/mcp.rs put_mcp_server_access). Example: a tool_grant is set to expire today at 2026-07-12T00:00:00+00:00 ("revoke this by midnight of today"). Empirically verified with the actual production DB engine (Python's sqlite3, same semantics as SQLite used by sqlx): `SELECT '2026-07-12T00:00:00+00:00' > datetime('now')` returns 1 (true) even though `datetime('now')` is '2026-07-12 09:25:49', i.e. 9+ hours past the intended expiry. Root cause: SQLite's datetime('now') always renders 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' with a SPACE at offset 10, while RFC3339 timestamps have 'T' (0x54) at offset 10; since 'T' > ' ' in ASCII, any expires_at whose date portion equals (or is later than) today's date always lexicographically compares greater than datetime('now'), regardless of the actual time-of-day. The grant/deny is therefore still resolved as "not expired" by resolve_explicit_permission -> resolve_tool_access (the core MCP permission gate) until the calendar date rolls over past midnight, silently extending a supposedly time-limited access grant for up to ~24 hours beyond its configured expiry. Fix direction: Normalize both sides to a comparable representation before comparing, e.g. `AND (expires_at IS NULL OR datetime(expires_at) > datetime('now'))` (SQLite's datetime() function parses ISO-8601/RFC3339 input and re-renders it in the canonical space-separated form so both operands compare correctly), or switch to `unixepoch(expires_at) > unixepoch('now')` / `julianday(expires_at) > julianday('now')`. Apply the same fix to both occurrences (lines 533 and 556).

issues.summary: LOW (latent): Permission-expiry check compares RFC3339 timestamps against SQLite datetime('now'), making same-day expiries ineffective — `is_permission_approved` (used by managers/mcp.rs to gate MCP server permission grants) treats any permission whose expiry falls on the current UTC calendar day as still valid until midnight, regardless of the actual expiry time, because of a string-format mismatch between chrono's RFC3339 output and SQLite's space-separated datetime('now') format. This silently defeats the intended time-limited-grant security control. The identical pattern (`expires_at > datetime('now')`) also appears in crates/core/src/db/mcp.rs (lines 533, 556), confirming this is a systemic bug rather than a one-off typo. Currently latent in practice: every live caller of create_permission_request in managers/mcp.rs passes `expires_at: None`, so the buggy branch is not exercised by any code path today — but the mechanism is broken the moment any caller (present or future) supplies a same-day expiry.
issues.pattern: expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > datetime\('now'\)
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2: 26 subsystem+security finders -> dedup -> severity-tiered adversarial verify; final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): db-submodules). Failure scenario: A permission_requests row is created with expires_at stored via chrono's to_rfc3339() (format "2026-07-12T09:00:00+00:00", note the 'T' separator and '+00:00' offset). SQLite's datetime('now') returns "2026-07-12 15:00:00" (space separator, no offset). Lexicographic string comparison hits the differing character at the date/time boundary: 'T' (0x54) > ' ' (0x20), so `expires_at > datetime('now')` evaluates TRUE for ANY same-calendar-day expiry regardless of the actual time-of-day, even hours after the intended expiry. Verified directly: `sqlite3` in-memory query with expires_at='2026-07-12T00:00:01+00:00' and now='2026-07-12 09:30:38' returns 1 (i.e. "not expired") even though the grant should have lapsed 9.5 hours earlier. Only once the calendar date rolls over does the comparison start behaving correctly (date digits differ before the 'T'/' ' divergence point). Fix direction: Compare using SQLite's julianday()/unixepoch() on both sides (e.g. `strftime('%s', expires_at) < strftime('%s','now')`), or store/compare using a normalized format (e.g. Unix epoch integer, or `to_rfc3339_opts(SecondsFormat::Secs, true)` to match SQLite's ISO8601-with-'T' `datetime()` output) so the comparison is either fully numeric or uses a consistent separator/offset convention on both sides. [Reconciled 2026-07-12 full-verify: correctness lens CONFIRMED via live sqlite3 repro, refuted on reachability only — all live callers pass expires_at=None so currently unreachable. Kept as LOW latent; reachable sibling is bug-455.]

issues.summary: CRITICAL: process_loop re-injects derived events into its own bounded mpsc channel without spawning, risking self-deadlock of the sole event-dispatch task — EventProcessor::process_loop is the single reader of a bounded (capacity-100) mpsc channel, but two of its own event-handling branches (ThoughtResponse at line 304, McpCallbackRequested/external_message at line 594) synchronously `.send().await` a derived event back onto that same channel from within the reader's own task instead of spawning the send as a separate task. Once the channel fills up (many concurrent producers exist: per-agent SystemHandler tasks, MCP stderr/log forwarding, chat/cron injectors), this creates a genuine self-deadlock: the send can only complete once capacity frees, and capacity can only free via a `recv()` that this exact task cannot perform while blocked in `send()`. The entire kernel event-dispatch pipeline hangs, requiring a restart — a kernel-down condition reachable through normal, non-adversarial load rather than any exploit.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): events). Failure scenario: The kernel creates the event channel as `mpsc::channel::<EnvelopedEvent>(100)` (crates/core/src/lib.rs:487) and hands the single Receiver to `EventProcessor::process_loop` (events.rs:201-208), which is the ONLY task that ever calls `event_rx.recv()`. Inside that same task's event-handling body, on `ThoughtResponse` (line 304) and on `McpCallbackRequested{callback_type=="external_message"}` (line 594) it builds a derived `EnvelopedEvent` and does `event_tx.send(...).await` directly on a clone of the very channel it is reading from — not via `tokio::spawn` (contrast with `redispatch_plugin_event` in managers/registry.rs, which deliberately `tokio::spawn`s the requeue so it never blocks the dispatch loop). If the channel is already at its 100-slot capacity (plausible under normal load: SystemHandler spawns one task per agent turn that itself emits ToolInvoked/ThoughtResponse/AgenticLoopCompleted events via its own event_tx clone — see handlers/system.rs — plus MCP stderr/logging notifications forwarded inline from lib.rs's notification listener, plus chat/cron traffic, all funneling into the same 100-slot channel), `process_loop`'s send at line 304 or 594 blocks awaiting capacity. But capacity can only be freed by `process_loop` itself calling `event_rx.recv()` again, and it cannot do that because it is parked inside this very `.send().await`. The sole consumer of the kernel's event bus permanently hangs — no further events (chat, agent completions, MCP callbacks) are ever processed until the process is restarted. Fix direction: Wrap both self-referential sends (lines 304 and 594) in `tokio::spawn(async move { ... })`, mirroring the pattern already used for `redispatch_plugin_event` in managers/registry.rs, so process_loop never blocks on writing to the channel it alone drains. Alternatively, use `try_send` and explicitly handle/log the full-channel case (e.g. drop with a loud warning or use a secondary unbounded queue) rather than awaiting capacity synchronously inside the reader task. — FIXED 2026-07-13 (branch fix/audit-critical-high): vulnerable anchor removed; verify-issues [FIXED].

issues.summary: HIGH: Client-controlled message id used unsanitized in filesystem path for attachment storage — path traversal / arbitrary file write — post_message builds the on-disk attachment directory from the client-supplied `id` field of the POST body with no character/format validation (no UUID check, no rejection of `/` or `..`), then create_dir_all + write into it. This is a straightforward path-traversal-to-arbitrary-file-write primitive reachable through the normal authenticated chat-message endpoint whenever an image content block exceeds the 64KB inline threshold (forcing the disk-storage branch). The filename component itself is safely derived from a server-generated UUID + allow-listed extension, but the containing directory is not.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): llm-proxy). Failure scenario: POST /api/chat/:agent_id/messages with body {"id": "../../../../Users/victim/Library/LaunchAgents", "source":"user", "content":[{"type":"image","url":"data:image/png;base64,<>65KB payload>"}]} (auth via the normal X-API-Key). `msg.id` is `payload.id` from the request body (PostMessageRequest.id, line 66) with zero validation anywhere in post_message. It flows straight into `let dir = state.data_dir.join("attachments").join(&msg.id)` (line 197) then `tokio::fs::create_dir_all(&dir)` (line 199) and `tokio::fs::write(&path, &decoded)` (line 203). Because `PathBuf::join` resolves `..` segments at the OS layer and fully replaces the base when the joined component is absolute, an attacker-chosen id lets them create directories and write attacker-controlled bytes (any base64 payload whose declared MIME string matches the allow-list, content itself is never validated) to an arbitrary filesystem path reachable by the ClotoCore process — e.g. `~/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, or any writable config/startup location, a path to persistence/RCE. Fix direction: Never fold client input into filesystem paths. Use the server-generated `att_id` (already minted at line 181) as the attachment subdirectory instead of `msg.id`, or at minimum canonicalize the resulting path and verify it is still a descendant of `state.data_dir.join("attachments")` before create_dir_all/write, rejecting otherwise. — FIXED 2026-07-13 (branch fix/audit-critical-high): vulnerable anchor removed; verify-issues [FIXED].

issues.summary: HIGH: Plugin FileRead/FileWrite capabilities all resolve to one shared, unscoped sandbox directory — SandboxedFileCapability::read_only/read_write is always constructed with the literal path `data/plugin_sandbox`, identical for every plugin regardless of identity, so the 'sandbox' is really one shared directory pooled across all plugins that hold FileRead or FileWrite. This breaks §1.5 Strict Permission Isolation's premise that a capability grant creates a secure execution boundary — the boundary here is only capability-type-wide (file vs. network), not plugin-wide, so any two plugins with overlapping file permissions can read/tamper with each other's data.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): capabilities-consensus). Failure scenario: get_capability_for_permission (lines 63-93) is invoked from the PermissionGranted event handler without the requesting plugin's id ever entering the sandbox path — both the FileRead branch (line 73) and the FileWrite branch (line 80) hard-code the literal `data/plugin_sandbox` as base_dir for every plugin. Concretely: an admin grants FileWrite to Plugin A and, separately, FileRead to Plugin B (an ordinary, expected §2.2 human-in-the-loop event, not an attack). Plugin A writes `state.json`/`cache.db` into its sandbox via the FileCapability::write it was handed. Plugin B, holding only FileRead, calls read("state.json") on ITS OWN capability object and receives Plugin A's file contents verbatim, because both capability objects are SandboxedFileCapability instances rooted at the exact same canonicalized directory. Any two plugins that are ever granted FileRead/FileWrite (whether cooperating, unrelated, or one of them malicious/compromised) can read and overwrite each other's files as long as they know or guess a filename — there is no per-plugin namespace despite the capability object nominally being 'sandboxed'. Fix direction: Thread the requesting plugin_id through get_capability_for_permission (and its caller in events.rs) and construct the sandbox base_dir per plugin, e.g. `data/plugin_sandbox/<plugin_id>/`, creating the directory on first use so each plugin's file capability is isolated from every other plugin's. — FIXED 2026-07-13 (branch fix/audit-critical-high): vulnerable anchor removed; verify-issues [FIXED].

issues.summary: HIGH: save_language_pack writes attacker-controlled content to an attacker-chosen absolute path (arbitrary file write) — `save_language_pack(filename, content)` is a #[tauri::command] with no capability/ACL scoping (not present in capabilities/default.json, unlike the fs plugin's scoped commands) and no server-side sanitization of `filename`. It is reachable end-to-end from the app's own 'import language pack' feature, where `filename` is the `code` field read straight out of the imported JSON — fully attacker-controlled. Because `PathBuf::join` replaces the whole path when given an absolute component, and `..` segments are not rejected either, this yields an arbitrary-path, arbitrary-content file write with only the .json suffix mandated.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): tauri-shell). Failure scenario: The 'Import language pack' feature (Settings > General) lets the user pick any JSON file via a native dialog; `importLanguagePack()` (dashboard/src/i18n.ts:136-159) parses that file and calls `savePack(pack.code, json)` -> `invoke('save_language_pack', {filename: pack.code, content: json})` with zero validation of `pack.code`. The Rust command joins `filename` (fully attacker-controlled, taken verbatim from the imported file's `code` field) with the languages dir via `dir.join(format!("{}.json", filename))`. Rust's `Path::join`/`PathBuf::push` documented behavior is that joining an absolute path *replaces* the base entirely, so `filename = "/Users/victim/Library/LaunchAgents/x"` yields the write target `/Users/victim/Library/LaunchAgents/x.json` — completely outside `Documents/ClotoCore/languages`, at a path chosen entirely by whoever authored the imported .json 'translation' file, with content also chosen by that file. A user importing a community-shared translation pack (the app's own advertised import flow) triggers an uncontrolled file write anywhere the process can write, no confirmation of the resulting path is ever shown. Fix direction: Reject `filename` values containing path separators or `..`, or better, derive the on-disk name from a generated/sanitized slug (allow only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`) rather than trusting the imported pack's `code` field directly; canonicalize the final path and verify with `starts_with(dir)` before writing. Apply the same fix to remove_language_pack. — FIXED 2026-07-13 (branch fix/audit-critical-high): vulnerable anchor removed; verify-issues [FIXED].

issues.summary: HIGH: ChatInputBar's edit-mode effect depends on an unstable object literal, silently reverting in-progress edits on any unrelated parent re-render — The prefill effect for edit-mode is meant to run once per edit session (keyed by `messageId`), but its dependency array also includes the unstable `editMode` object itself. Since the caller constructs that object as a fresh literal on every render, the effect re-runs on every parent re-render while editing is active, resetting the input text to the original (pre-edit) content and discarding the user's in-progress edit.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): dash-agent-chat). Failure scenario: AgentConsole passes `editMode={editingMessage ? { messageId, initialContent, onCancel: () => setEditingMessage(null) } : null}` inline (AgentConsole.tsx lines 1059-1072) — a brand new object/closure on every AgentConsole render, even when `editingMessage` itself hasn't changed. AgentConsole re-renders during an active edit session whenever unrelated state changes, e.g. `setPendingApprovals` in the unconditional `if (event.type === 'CommandApprovalResult') { setPendingApprovals(...) }` handler (line 465-467) fires for ANY agent's approval resolving system-wide, not just this one. Because ChatInputBar's useEffect dependency array includes the whole `editMode` object (not just `editMode?.messageId`), the reference change re-triggers the effect, calling `setInput(editMode.initialContent)` again — wiping out whatever the user has typed into the edit box back to the pre-edit original text, and re-firing the 50ms `focus()` timer. Fix direction: Drop `editMode` from the dependency array and depend only on the stable primitive `editMode?.messageId` (already present), or memoize the `editMode` object in AgentConsole with `useMemo` keyed on `editingMessage?.id`. — FIXED 2026-07-13 (branch fix/audit-critical-high): vulnerable anchor removed; verify-issues [FIXED].

issues.summary: MEDIUM: PUT /api/plugins/:id/config broadcasts the plaintext plugin config (potentially containing an API key) over the kernel event bus, which is streamed unmasked to every SSE client and persisted for replay — Unlike every other secret-touching endpoint in this codebase (`list_llm_providers` masks with `has_key`, `get_mcp_server_settings` masks KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD/CREDENTIAL env values with `***`, `redact_secrets()` scrubs upstream error text), `update_plugin_config` has no masking at all: it fetches the raw config row and puts it straight into a kernel event that gets broadcast to the shared SSE channel and cached in the replay history buffer. Any client holding a valid session token that is connected to (or later reconnects to) `/api/events/stream` receives the plaintext secret, and it lingers in the in-process `event_history` ring buffer for the retention window, unlike the request/response pair which is not logged anywhere else.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): sec-secrets). Failure scenario: An admin sets a secret via `PUT /api/plugins/:id/config` with body `{"key": "api_key", "value": "sk-..."}` (this is literally the documented example payload, doc comment: 'Config may contain sensitive values (API keys, tokens)'). `update_plugin_config` re-reads the full unmasked config from `plugin_configs` (crates/core/src/managers/plugin.rs `get_config`, no redaction) and embeds it verbatim in a `ClotoEventData::ConfigUpdated{plugin_id, config}` event, then sends it on `state.event_tx`. `EventProcessor::process_loop` (crates/core/src/events.rs:254-260) immediately rebroadcasts every non-ActionRequested/PermissionGranted event on `tx_internal`, which is the exact same `broadcast::Sender<SequencedEvent>` (`state.tx`, wired at crates/core/src/lib.rs:727) that `sse_handler` (crates/core/src/handlers.rs:287) subscribes to for `GET /api/events/stream`. The event is also written into `event_history` (crates/core/src/events.rs:213-214) before broadcast, so any future SSE client that reconnects with an older `Last-Event-ID` receives the plaintext secret via history replay (crates/core/src/handlers.rs:293-306), well after the original request. Fix direction: Before building the `ConfigUpdated` envelope, mask sensitive keys in `full_config` the same way `get_mcp_server_settings` does (case-insensitive KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD/CREDENTIAL substring match → `***`), or omit the `config` payload from the broadcast event entirely and have interested subscribers re-fetch via the already-authenticated `GET /api/plugins/:id/config` endpoint (which itself should also mask before this is fully fixed, since it likewise returns `full_config`/`config` unmasked to any caller with the admin key).

issues.summary: MEDIUM: Auto-generated .env containing CLOTO_API_KEY is left world-readable on Windows installs — The .env permission hardening added to protect the auto-generated admin API key is gated behind `#[cfg(unix)]` with no Windows counterpart, so on a Windows install the secret file inherits the default (often multi-user-readable) ACL of the install prefix, letting another local user harvest the admin key.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): config-scheduler). Failure scenario: `install()` writes a freshly generated 64-hex-char `CLOTO_API_KEY` (the admin secret the .env template itself documents as 'REQUIRED: Without this, all admin operations are denied') into `<prefix>/.env`, then restricts the file to 0600 only inside a `#[cfg(unix)]` block. On Windows there is no equivalent hardening anywhere in the codebase (`crates/core/src/platform/windows.rs::set_executable_permission` is an unrelated no-op, and no ACL-tightening call exists for `.env`). The Windows default install prefix from `cli.rs::default_prefix()` is `C:\ProgramData\Cloto`, a directory that by default grants the local `Users` group read access. Any other local, unprivileged Windows account on the same machine (or a service running under a different account) can therefore read `<prefix>\.env` and obtain the admin API key, gaining full admin REST API access to the running ClotoCore instance (plugin config, permissions, shutdown, etc.) even though the kernel binds to loopback by default. Fix direction: Add a Windows-specific ACL tightening step (e.g. via `icacls` or the Windows security APIs) in `platform/windows.rs` analogous to the Unix `0o600` chmod, and call it from `installer.rs` regardless of platform (replace the `#[cfg(unix)]`-only block with a `crate::platform::restrict_secret_file_permission(&env_path)` call implemented per-OS).

issues.summary: MEDIUM: LLM proxy relays raw upstream error bodies (potential API-key echoes) back to MCP subprocess callers and into logs, unredacted — proxy_handler's error-relay path forwards the raw upstream error JSON body (resp_body) both into a tracing::warn! log and into the response returned to the MCP-server caller, without ever calling the redaction routine that already exists elsewhere in this codebase for the identical risk (llm.rs::redact_secrets, used only for the admin dashboard's test_provider_connection endpoint). Since llm_proxy.rs's entire raison d'être is keeping API keys away from MCP subprocesses, any upstream provider that echoes back key material in its error response defeats that guarantee.
issues.notes: Discovered by ClotoCore comprehensive code-quality audit 2026-07-12 (an earlier decision / an earlier decision; Sonnet-5 Workflow wf_3a2b40c2-649 resume: 26 finders -> dedup 63 -> severity-tiered adversarial verify (all 160 agents, 0 error); final verdict CONFIRMED; finder(s): llm-proxy). Failure scenario: A provider returns a 401/403/etc with the invalid/expired key echoed in the error body (a documented real pattern — see llm.rs's own redact_secrets() doc comment: "upstream error bodies sometimes echo the key back verbatim"). proxy_handler logs the whole body verbatim via `warn!(... body = %resp_body ...)` (line 312) and then extracts `upstream_detail` straight from `resp_body` (lines 351-356) into `full_msg`, which is returned in the JSON error response body to the calling Mind MCP server subprocess. This directly contradicts the file's own stated purpose: "This ensures API keys are never exposed to MCP server subprocesses" (module doc, lines 3-5) — the exact mitigation (`redact_secrets`) already exists in llm.rs for the admin-facing surface but is never applied here on the more security-critical, MCP-subprocess-facing path. Fix direction: Scrub `provider.api_key` (and any other secret material) out of `resp_body`/`upstream_detail` before logging or returning it, e.g. reuse (or move to shared code) the `redact_secrets` helper from handlers/llm.rs on both the warn! call and the response body.
